THOUGHT: This 44-year-old female presents with acute-onset confusion, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and fatigue — all beginning after eating. Critically, her serum glucose is profoundly low at 41 mg/dL (hypoglycemia), and she has a history of diabetes and recent sleeve gastrectomy (1 month ago). Post-bariatric hypoglycemia — particularly postprandial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (PHH) — is a well-recognized complication following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and, increasingly recognized, after sleeve gastrectomy. Although less common after sleeve, PHH can occur due to accelerated gastric emptying, exaggerated GLP-1 and GIP secretion, and subsequent inappropriate insulin hypersecretion from pancreatic beta cells. Her normal C-peptide level confirms endogenous insulin production (i.e., not exogenous insulin overdose or factitious hypoglycemia), supporting reactive/hyperinsulinemic etiology. The confusion is a classic neuroglycopenic symptom of hypoglycemia; autonomic symptoms (e.g., tachycardia — HR 120) and GI symptoms (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) are also commonly reported in PHH, likely mediated by catecholamine surges and gut hormone effects. Her hypotension (BP 104/54) and tachycardia further support adrenergic response to hypoglycemia. Other causes of hypoglycemia (e.g., insulinoma) are less likely given the temporal association with meals, recent surgery, and absence of fasting hypoglycemia (no mention of overnight fasting symptoms); additionally, insulinomas typically present with fasting hypoglycemia and elevated C-peptide (here, C-peptide is normal — though “normal” does not exclude mild hyperinsulinism, especially if drawn during recovery phase). Non-hypoglycemic causes of confusion (e.g., stroke, infection, metabolic encephalopathy) are less likely: no fever, normal WBC/CRP not provided but no signs of systemic infection; neuro exam shows no focal deficits; electrolytes are normal (Na 139, K 3.9, HCO3 24), BUN/Cr suggest mild prerenal azotemia possibly from volume depletion due to vomiting/diarrhea — but not severe enough to cause encephalopathy. Her depression/suicide history raises concern for intentional overdose, but no toxidrome, normal electrolytes, and normal C-peptide argue against sulfonylurea or insulin ingestion (which would elevate C-peptide in sulfonylurea use, and cause very low C-peptide in exogenous insulin use). Thus, the most coherent, temporally aligned, and pathophysiologically plausible diagnosis is post-bariatric (sleeve gastrectomy–associated) hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

DIAGNOSIS: Postprandial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia following sleeve gastrectomy
